analysis.one_liner: Requires the President, Vice President, and Members of Congress to put their stocks and securities in blind trusts.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in December 2011, was sent to two House committees and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend federal ethics law to force the President, Vice President, and every Member of Congress to hand their stocks, bonds, and commodities futures to a qualified blind trust, meaning an independent trustee controls the investments and the officeholder no longer knows what they own. Lawmakers would have 30 days to comply, with a possible 30-day extension. It exempts federal retirement accounts and Social Security benefits. The Attorney General could sue an official who knowingly ignores the rule, with a civil penalty of up to $50,000.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyday investors and the general public, who gain greater assurance that elected officials cannot use nonpublic information from their jobs to trade securities for personal profit. It also protects officials themselves by removing the appearance and opportunity of conflicts of interest.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary investors and the general public

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires the President, Vice President, and each Member of Congress to place all stocks, bonds, commodities futures, and other securities — including those held jointly with a spouse — in a qualified blind trust, so they no longer control what they own while in office [S2][S3].

Officials must comply within 30 days of taking office or of the law's enactment, with only one 30-day extension available, limiting the window during which they can keep trading personal portfolios [S2][S3].

The Attorney General is authorized to bring a civil action against any covered official who knowingly and willfully fails to comply, with a court able to impose a penalty of up to $50,000, giving the rule actual legal teeth [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress, the President, and the Vice President who hold securities would bear the cost: they would surrender control of their investment portfolios and pay blind-trust administrative fees. Officials with large holdings have the most money at stake.

drawbacks.text: The penalty for knowingly defying the rule is capped at $50,000, a sum that may be small relative to the portfolios of senior officials, and enforcement depends entirely on the Attorney General of the day choosing to sue [S3].

The bill allows one 30-day extension for compliance and exempts federal retirement plans and Social Security benefits, so officials retain some financial interests outside the blind trust, and blind trusts can hold diversified funds whose overall value still rises or falls with policy outcomes [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to public confidence and market fairness come at a modest, well-defined cost to the officials covered: loss of control over their personal investments and administrative trust fees. The main weaknesses are the light $50,000 penalty and reliance on the Attorney General to enforce it. On balance it is a straightforward anti-corruption rule whose costs fall almost entirely on the officials it regulates.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Oversight and Government Reform and House Administration committees in December 2011, neither committee ever acted on it, and it died when that Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Rep. Richard Nugent introduced the bill on December 13, 2011, and it was referred to the Committee on Oversight and Government Reform and the Committee on House Administration [S1][S5].
The bill was never reported out of either committee: the action history shows no hearings, markups, floor scheduling, or votes after the initial referral [S5].
The bill died when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Members of Congress and executive officials who hold securities are better off, because they kept the ability to manage and trade their own portfolios without a blind-trust requirement. No countermeasure from this bill advanced instead.

for.name: Rep. Richard B. Nugent
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Prevent Insider Trading by Elected Officials Act on December 13, 2011.

for.name: 5 Republican House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it small-bloc support but no Democratic cosponsors.

against.name: House Oversight and Government Reform Committee
against.role: One of two committees of referral; chaired by Rep. Darrell Issa (R-CA)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral but never held a markup or reported the bill out.

against.name: House Committee on House Administration
against.role: Second committee of referral; chaired by Rep. Dan Lungren (R-CA)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral but took no further action on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all five cosponsors were Republicans, and the bill never reached a vote, so no party split on the merits was ever recorded.

industries.industry: Members of Congress and executive officials with securities holdings
industries.note: The bill would force these officeholders to hand their stock, bond, and commodities-futures portfolios to blind trusts, ending their ability to trade while in office. Their personal financial interest in continued discretionary trading runs against the public's interest in officials not trading on privileged information.
